12.0.0.en: "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" [1]

12.0.1.en: He who accepts discipline desires the truth. But he who hates reproof is like a (brutish) animal that cannot appreciate correction (Prov 10:17). He prefers his unbridled will, even if it is against sound teaching. Acceptance of discipline is a sincere sign of the desire for progress and correction, and therefore of the desire to enjoy true knowledge. The psalmist says: "Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil for the head" (Ps 141:5). And the Apostle Paul says: "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby" (Heb 12:11).

12.0.2.en: He who refuses discipline is like the animal that kicks or bites the one who offers it medicines for healing, because it does not understand what lies behind the pain, but seeks temporary comfort even at the expense of its health and benefit.

12.0.3.en: * I am obliged to exhort you, and especially to use reproof with you. For just as fire melts wax, so the fear of punishments softens the hearts of sinners, and not only this, but it burns up your sins through your repentance and your return to the Redeemer, and enriches your minds and increases your boldness and your striving.

12.0.4.en: * This is counsel, not judgment; medicine, not punishment; correction, not torture... a spiritual remedy to heal sinners and keep them from new sins.

12.0.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Discipline (or reproof) is a proof of loving care, and it leads to understanding.

12.0.6.en: The Teacher shows this reproof when He says in Scripture: "How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37).

12.0.7.en: Scripture also says: "They went a whoring after idols and stones, and offered their burnt offerings to Baal." It is a great proof of His love, for although He knows the shame of those who rejected Him and that they ran far from Him, yet He urges them to repent... In His care for the people He rebuked them in Isaiah, saying: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isa 29:13). And He says also: "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men" (Mt 15:9). Here His loving care shows their sins and their salvation side by side.

12.1.s.en: 2. The good man and the man of devices

12.1.0.en: 2 A good man obtaineth favour of the LORD: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn. 3 A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved.

12.1.1.en: "A good man obtaineth favour of the LORD: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn" [2]

12.1.2.en: The good man obtains grace and benefit from the Lord, because all the goodness in him is not from himself, but is the Lord's gift to him through free grace. And as he submits to Him in obedience, his goodness grows and increases. But the goodness of God is absolute by nature, and does not change.

12.1.3.en: Some see that the literal translation of the word "favour" is "good will," for it is from the Lord.

12.1.4.en: We do nothing good by ourselves, but by the will of God we receive this salvation; and we are called (saints) not because we deserve it, but because in that is His good pleasure.

12.1.5.en: St. John Chrysostom If other things are found called good in the Holy Bible, such as an angel (Tob 5:21; 2 Macc 11:6), or a man (Prov 12:2; Ps 37:23; Mt 12:35), or a servant (Sir 7:21; Lk 19:17), or a treasure (Tob 4:9; Lk 6:45), or a good heart (Jdt 8:28; Wis 1:1; Sir 26:4; Lk 8:15), or a good tree (2 Kgs 3:19; Mt 7:17-19), all these were so called by an inexact use of the word, since the goodness in them is incidental and not essential.

12.1.6.en: * Christ is the Good that the people were awaiting.

12.1.7.en: Origen * If you do good you live in God, and those who do good like you live also.

12.1.8.en: Hermas "A man of devices" does not mean only one who devises plots by deeds and words, but one who carries in his heart or mind the desire to devise plots against his brother, even if he does not accomplish it because of the inadequacy of his means.

12.1.9.en: The face of the Lord shines on the good man, and so the man becomes steadfast and unshaken (Rom 14:4). But the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous (Ps 1:5). [Cf. Hushai and Ahithophel (2 Sam 15:32; 16:15; 17:23).]

12.1.10.en: * The righteous man dies in the strength of his simplicity, in complete mastery over his will, with a soul full as of meadows. But the sinner, though he lives in comfort, giving off sweet perfumes, ends his life in the bitterness of his soul, and passes his last day without taking anything of the good things he once enjoyed, carrying nothing but the wages of his evil.

12.1.11.en: * St. Job answers: Do not think that you are happy while you are immersed in pleasures, because the blows of God have not fallen on you in this life. "The lamp of the wicked shall be put out." It gives light for a time, but it carries no eternal light. And although the world favors such people because they practice the will of God, who has authority over the world (Jn 14:30), yet there usually comes a moment of change in events, when sorrows come from the wrath and anger of heaven, when the wicked are sifted "as stubble before the wind." The unjust are sifted like straw, and the righteous like wheat. Look to the Lord who says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32).

12.2.0.en: St. Ambrose "A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved" [3]

12.2.1.en: * The man who founds his life on evil is like one who builds his house on the sand, as the Lord Christ says, and the rain descends, and the floods come, and the winds blow, and beat upon that house, and it falls, and great is the fall of it (Mt 7:27). But the wise righteous man founds his life on the Lord Christ, the Rock, and the rain descends, and the floods come, and the winds blow, and beat upon that house, and it will not be shaken.

12.2.2.en: The overflow of rivers, as in the lands of Egypt and Assyria, cannot harm them; rather, those who build on the sand, that is, who practice the wisdom of the world, are the ones harmed. The winds that blow are like false prophets. All these come together in one place and strike the house. But if it is founded on the rock, no harm comes to them, for there is no way of a serpent upon a rock (Prov 30:19).

12.2.3.en: Origen * Those who hear the words of the Lord are like a wise man who builds on the rock. Those who do not follow the words of the Lord are like a foolish man who builds his house on the sand.

12.2.4.en: * He who practices virtue becomes able through Christ who strengthens him (Phil 4:13). We receive everything from God, who puts all things in their place. From Him come wisdom, insight and union with all that is good.

12.2.5.en: * The wicked man cannot accuse God as the cause of his evils and his folly. He makes himself like a fool when he withdraws from what proceeds to him according to nature, and turns aside to what is contrary to nature.

12.2.6.en: St. Cyril the Great * Jesus speaks of human circumstances and calamities by way of reference to rain, flood and winds, such as false accusations, plunder, death, the loss of family members, insults from others, and all the horrible things in life that a man can speak of. And Jesus says that the soul that follows the way of loftiness does not yield to these disasters that may happen. The secret of this is that the soul is founded on the rock.

12.2.7.en: The "rock" signifies reliance on the teachings of our Lord Jesus, for His commandments are stronger than any rock. They are founded in calm above all the human waves of life. He who keeps these commandments carefully rises, not only above human beings when they teach them with malice, but even above the demons themselves with their plans.

12.3.s.en: 3. The virtuous woman and the woman who shames

12.3.0.en: "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones" [4]

12.3.1.en: It is dangerous to limit virtue to virginity alone. The virtuous woman radiates many qualities, as is stated in (Prov 31). She is truly the crown of her husband. But the foolish and lazy woman causes him shame, and brings him down to old age.

12.3.2.en: * The crown of the woman must be reckoned her husband, and the crown of the husband is his marriage, for both have the flower of their union, which is the child, truly the meadows of the flesh. The crown of the old is their grandchildren, and the glory of children is their fathers, as it is said (cf. Prov 17:6). Our glory is the Father of all, and the crown of the whole Church is Christ.

12.3.3.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * When you go to choose a wife, look not only for a companion for you in life, but also for a companion for you in virtue.

12.3.4.en: It is inevitable that the husband of a corrupt woman perishes with her in her way. Therefore look to virtue, not to money. Then the virtuous wife becomes a crown of glory, because she is strong. But the wicked one is like a worm dwelling in his heart, causing gradual ruin in silence.

12.3.5.en: What is more dangerous than this? She does not appear outwardly, but this kind of wife injects poison into the wretched soul and destroys it. On the contrary, virtue adorns him who follows it, while evil burdens the wicked man with more hatred.

12.3.6.en: St. John Chrysostom How great the difference between devout Sarah, who shared her husband's good life, and Job's wife, who asked him to curse God and die! The Apostle Peter says: "Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement."

12.3.7.en: * When they (the man and his wife) are in agreement, and their children in good upbringing, and their household in good order, the neighbors smell the sweet fragrance of the harmony, and with them the friends and relatives. But if it is otherwise, everything is overturned and falls into confusion.

12.4.s.en: 4. The thoughts and counsels of the righteous and the wicked

12.4.0.en: 5 The thoughts of the righteous are right: but the counsels of the wicked are deceit. 6 The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them. 7 The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand. 8 A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised.

12.4.1.en: "The thoughts of the righteous are right: but the counsels of the wicked are deceit" [5]

12.4.2.en: The thoughts of the righteous are simple and clear, aiming at what builds up the soul and others, so they are upright in the eyes of God and men. Good thoughts are translated into good words and righteous conduct, and are rewarded by God who loves righteousness and goodness. But the thoughts of the wicked are mixed with cheating and deceit at the expense of their neighbors as well as themselves, for they perish because of them..

12.4.3.en: * Thoughts come from ourselves, since by nature we remember what we do or have done or have heard. Of this the blessed David says: "I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times. I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search" (Ps 77:5-6). Again he says: "The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity" (Ps 94:11), "The thoughts of the righteous are right..." (Prov 12:5). And in the Gospel the Lord says to the Pharisees: "Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?!" (Mt 9:4).

12.4.4.en: Father Moses * The more you are negligent in watching your mind (your thoughts), the greater the distance becomes between you and Jesus.

12.4.5.en: Hesychius of Jerusalem * By long observation we have found a difference between the thoughts that come from angels, the thoughts that come from men, and the thoughts that spring from Satan; that difference is:

12.4.6.en: The thoughts from the angels work to reveal the nature of things and their spiritual meanings. As, for example, they reveal:

12.4.7.en: For what purpose does gold exist?!

12.4.8.en: And why is it scattered like sand in the valleys?

12.4.9.en: And why do they obtain it with great toil and striving?

12.4.10.en: And how, when it is discovered, it is washed not with water but with fire, and after that is placed in the hands of craftsmen who fashion from it lampstands and censers for the house of God (2 Chr 19:4-21), those vessels which, by the grace of God, the king of Babylon was not able to use for himself (Dan 3:5), while Cleopas offers a heart burning with these mysteries (Lk 32:24).

12.4.11.en: But the thought that springs from the demons does not know this or understand it, but shamelessly presents only the possession of gold, deluding us with the pleasure and glory that we obtain by acquiring gold.

12.4.12.en: As for the (mere) human thought, it neither seeks the possession of gold nor yearns to understand the (spiritual) meanings (of its existence and of its use for good...), but presents to the mind the images of gold without lusts or covetousness.

12.4.13.en: And if a man applies this with his mind to other things (besides gold), he will find the same.

12.5.0.en: St. Evagrius "The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them" [6]

12.5.1.en: The wicked cast their words with malice, as though they were nets to catch others and shed their blood. But the upright offer their words to rescue themselves from the nets set for them by the wicked.

12.5.2.en: The Pharisees tried to trap the Lord Christ with their words, and His answer came to silence them and nullify their wicked schemes. "Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk" (Mt 22:15; Mk 12:13; Lk 11:54).

12.5.3.en: * Keep your tongues from speaking evil of your brothers, for he who speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his companion he does to God.

12.5.4.en: * The soul of a man who is not perfect in the virtues is found pure like the sun before an evil word reaches him, but if he hears an evil word or slander, immediately the demons overpower his mind and veil the light from him, and make him wretched because his soul is unsteady and his virtues incomplete.

12.5.5.en: St. Macarius the Great * An elder said: "The tongue is full of fire and it defiles the whole body, so let him who loves his life spare his tongue. Guard your lips, O man of God, and bridle your tongue, and you will profit from all your labors, for he who keeps his tongue has many honors, and blessed is he who rules over his tongue, for his storehouses (that is, his granaries) are filled with good things."

12.5.6.en: * An elder said: "If the movements of your tongue are abundant, the pure movements in your heart have been extinguished, but if your tongue is silent and your heart boils with pure movements, blessed are you, for its movement by the Spirit lifts you to the calm of life. Your tongue was silent that your heart might speak, and your heart was silent that the Spirit might speak in it."

12.6.0.en: The Paradise of the Fathers "The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand" [7]

12.6.1.en: The wicked may flourish, and appear successful and healthy, with children to inherit them and perpetuate their memory, but sooner or later evil sweeps them away, and they lose everything, and their souls perish. But the righteous, though they suffer trials and pains, their house stands.

12.6.2.en: When bitter trials came upon Job and he lost his sons and daughters at one stroke, his friends thought that this was a true and certain testimony of his grave wickedness and hypocrisy. But Job was glorified and enjoyed the sight of God, and received double what he had lost, and his memory is still alive to this day in heaven and on earth, as though his house were still standing, while as for his friends, the world knows nothing of them.

12.6.3.en: The two midwives whom Pharaoh asked to kill the male Hebrew children at their birth acted in the spirit of the fear of God; therefore it was said of them: "Therefore God dealt well with the midwives... And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses" (Ex 1:20-21). As Nathan the prophet said to David the king: "Also the LORD telleth thee that the LORD will make thee an house" (2 Sam 7:11). So when we enjoy the fear of the Lord, God Himself builds for us a spiritual house made by His own hands to dwell in Himself.

12.6.4.en: * Without the fear of God a house cannot be built. If by the fear of God houses were built by those who committed no sin, but raised their buildings according to the good pleasure of God, what shall we do, who have been taken captive (by sin)? Listen, O sinner: we must fear God in order to avoid sin, but after a loss has occurred to us and our ship has been wrecked, there is another lifeboat, and it is repentance.

12.6.5.en: St. Jerome Pope Gregory the Great holds that the wicked man, when he is overturned or changed, "is not," not in the sense that he loses his existence or his being, but that he no longer stands in the state of evil in which he was.

12.6.6.en: The wicked Pharaoh thought he was able to destroy the people of God, so he commanded that their children be cast into the river, and he did not realize that his evil would return upon his family after 80 years and destroy his army, while God works wonders for His people.

12.6.7.en: * Pharaoh commanded that the children be cast into the river. Had the children not been cast out, Moses would not have been brought into the palace. When the child Moses was safe he was not honored, and when he was cast into the river he became honored. God did that to show the riches of His means and ways.

12.7.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised" [8]

12.7.1.en: Nothing honors a man like heavenly wisdom, for it reflects upon him an inward heavenly splendor, and he carries within him the spirit of truth. All men prefer wisdom, and the world honors prudence and spiritual understanding, even though he who holds to these things is exposed to persecutions and opposition.

12.7.2.en: But the perverse man, who thinks himself wise and able to reach his goal by crooked ways, is not pleasing to God, and even men discover the truth of his character and make light of him, and mock his crooked manner.

12.7.3.en: * Heartbreaking and deadly is this poison of the enemy, by which he has blinded many and cast them down suddenly, for he suggests to the soul a false and ruinous thought, so that it imagines it has attained things not attained by most people, and that it excels in fasting. He also suggests to the soul many heroic deeds, and leads it astray by making it forget all its sins so that it feels its superiority over those around it. He steals from its heart the remembrance of its faults, and he does this not for the soul's benefit, but so that it may not be able to utter this healing saying: "Against thee only have I sinned; have mercy upon me" (Ps 51:4, 1), and he does not allow it to say: "I will praise the LORD with my whole heart" (Ps 111:1). Rather, as Satan himself said in his heart: "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God" (Isa 14:13), so he deceives man by turning him toward domination and high positions, and also toward the positions of teaching and boasting of healing. And so the soul perishes by deception, being struck with a wound hard to heal.

12.7.4.en: Amma Syncletica * Do not receive vainglory into yourself, for you cannot bear its deceit and the madness of its hypocrisy, since it brings deceitful thoughts upon you.

12.7.5.en: * If you surrender your heart to it in false dreams, it grows more firmly rooted in vain thought until it misleads all who receive the spirit that loves the saying written of it: "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 14:8).

12.8.0.en: "He that is despised, and hath a servant, is better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread" [v. 9].

12.8.1.en: He says that the man who appears despised, without reputation or fame, and without the show of greatness and pomp, but who has a servant or slave who renders him humble service, is better than he who glorifies himself and cares for vain greatness and has nothing to live on, not even the necessities. When Saul wished to give his daughter to David as a wife, David did not exalt himself, but said to the king's servants: "Seemeth it to you a light thing to be a king's son in law, seeing that I am a poor and needy man?" (1 Sam 18:23).

12.8.2.en: The Latin translation (the Vulgate) reads: "Better is the poor man who supports himself than the proud man who lacks bread."

12.8.3.en: The proverb in general means that it is better for a man to appear poor while his depths lack nothing than a man who is occupied with outward appearances and vainglory and suffers emptiness.

12.8.4.en: * In these snares the weak fall... for while they are indifferent to their own salvation, and while they themselves need the teaching and guidance of others, they are deceived by the wiles of Satan under the cover of guiding others and urging them to repentance. So if they obtain some gain from their talk with others, they lose their patience in the matters that must be acquired. And so there comes upon them what Haggai the prophet said: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6). For truly the man who puts his wages in a bag with holes loses all that he seemed to have gained from his talk with others, because of the loss of his self-control and his mental confusion every day. The result is that while he thinks he can acquire great gain by teaching others, he in truth deprives himself of growth, for "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches," "He that is despised, and hath a servant, is better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread" (Prov 13:7; 12:9).

12.8.5.en: Father Abraham * If you clothe yourself with poverty in this world together with humility, you will be with the Son of God in His Kingdom.

12.8.6.en: * Blessed is the poor and needy who keeps stillness. He will be a friend of God like Abraham, for the Lord does nothing unless He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets (Amos 9:3).

12.8.7.en: * Let your labor be between you and God, until God makes it manifest at the resurrection and glorifies you for it among all the righteous and the just.

12.8.8.en: * Do not receive vainglory into yourself, for you cannot bear its deceit and the madness of its hypocrisy, since it brings deceitful thoughts upon you.

12.8.9.en: * O poor one, acquire patience and be humble, and you will attain this honor. And let your heart think on heavenly things and not on things on the earth. And be confident that the saints will come to you. And imitate the disciples of Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power forever. Amen.

12.9.s.en: 6. The mercies of the righteous and the cruelty of the wicked

12.9.0.en: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel" [v. 10].

12.9.1.en: The righteous man cannot but be gentle even with animals. But the wicked man becomes a beast of prey when he obtains authority over others. Violence and evil are brothers who work together.

12.9.2.en: * "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." It is a training in human tenderness, when a person becomes accustomed to showing mercy to his fellow men through practicing it on his animals. Surely he who is tender toward animals is all the more inclined to be tender toward his brothers... Do the righteous have compassion on the souls of their animals? Never! For certainly benefits must be conveyed to them, and so much the more should he practice that with his fellow men. God rightly commanded us to care for wounded animals and to return the strayed ones, and not to muzzle the ox (Deut 22:1-4). He asks us to keep animals in complete safety, first for our own sake, and second so that they may serve us. At the same time this is a training in caring for others and doing what is useful to them. Truly he who has compassion on strangers will all the more have compassion on those he knows. And he who is tender to his servants will be all the more tender to his brothers. Perhaps you will say: The animal gives you useful service, but in what does your brother benefit you? I say that he is a greater help to you than it, and that in the sight of God. You can see this when we care for our animals in this way, we do not count it a lowly work. For in doing this we serve not them alone but ourselves also.

12.9.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * When any man acquires the love of goodness of which we have spoken, by which we become like God, then he is given the tender heart of God, and he prays for those who wrong him, saying in the same pattern: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).

12.9.4.en: There is a clear sign that reveals the soul that has not yet been wholly purified of the residue of sin, and it is that it does not grieve tenderly over the faults of others, but judges them like a judge in fierce blame.

12.9.5.en: But how can he attain perfect purity of heart who does not carry out the commandments which the Apostle sets forth, "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2), and who has not the virtue of love, which "doth not behave itself unseemly... is not easily provoked... thinketh no evil... beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 13:4-7)?! For "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel" (Prov 12:10).

12.9.6.en: So the man (the monk) falls into the very faults for which he cruelly and without gentleness condemns another, for "A wicked messenger falleth into mischief" (Prov 13:17), and "Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard" (Prov 21:13).

12.9.7.en: Father Cheremon St. Augustine asks us to have the quarrels of doves and not the kisses of wolves. For doves, even in their quarrel, do not hurt one another, but use their beaks to attack the other's beak without harm, and after the quarrel the doves fly together and eat together in harmony. But wolves, even if you want to kiss them, attack and hurt. So the believer carries tenderness toward all, and the wicked man overflows with violence and cruelty.

12.9.8.en: * He who uses violence is worse than he who steals.

12.9.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * You have been commanded to rescue the ass or the ox that has fallen in the mud. Do you see a Christian like yourself, saved by the blood of Christ, cast into the sewer of drunkenness, and wallowing in the mire of dissipation, and you stand silent? Do you pass by and stretch out no hand of mercy? Do you stop at crying out and rebuking, or do you tremble for him?

12.9.10.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * If the Law does not allow you to separate the young irrational animal from its mother before it has suckled (Lev 22:27 etc.), how much more must mankind be prepared against violence.

12.10.0.en: "He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding" [11].

12.10.1.en: The word of God is a field that needs continual tilling (2 Tim 2:15). Every moment we devote to the word of God has its fruit in due time. But he who wastes his time on unseemly things does not enjoy true knowledge, because he does not till the field of the Holy Bible, and so he is deprived of the bread of the word.

12.10.2.en: It is fitting for the believer to plow the ground of Scripture every day, that he may be satisfied with the heavenly bread. For he who walks in the way of Scripture runs toward heaven and grows in every good work.

12.10.3.en: Timothy represents the man who grows through the word (2 Tim 3:14-17), and Jehoiakim represents the one who resists the word (Jer 36:22-32).

12.10.4.en: * It has come to my knowledge that a lazy man took the Holy Bible into his lap from the seventh hour (that is, one o'clock in the afternoon) until sunset and was not able to open it at all, as though he were bound with lead. But Anba Anthony did as the angel showed him: at one time he sat practicing his work, at another he rose to pray persistently, and at another he sat reading the words of God. And he was granted such enlightenment that he said to one of the philosophers of his time: [It is enough for me to contemplate the nature of creatures always, and to recite the sayings of the Lord until the darkness of night.] To this extent he was in touch with God, and his night shone like day, as it is said: "Even the darkness is not dark to thee, and the night shineth as the day" (Ps 139:12).

12.11.s.en: 8. The desires of the wicked are evil

12.11.0.en: 12 The wicked desireth the net of evil men: but the root of the righteous yieldeth fruit.

12.11.1.en: "The desires of the wicked are evil, and the root of the righteous is profitable" [v. 12 LXX]

12.11.2.en: The desires of the wicked are evil, as if he overflows with what is in his heart even upon his inward desires and his outward conduct. He is like one who casts nets in every place to catch evils, and he does not know that while he hunts them, they hunt him in their snares.

12.11.3.en: But the righteous man, being genuine in his thought and principles, moves with balance for the good of all, bears with them in love and does not condemn them.

12.11.4.en: * There was an honorable man who had a debtor, and he kept asking him for the debt for ten years and he did not answer him, and the creditor bore with him with a good heart. He had a friend, who said to him: "I am amazed at you, how is it that you have not grown resentful toward him, for you have been asking him for a long time and he has not responded?"

12.11.5.en: He said to him: "You wonder that I have been longsuffering with him for ten years, and behold, God has been asking me for more than fifty years to keep His commandments, and until now I have not responded to Him nor fulfilled His will, and He with a good heart bears with me. So if I, a man, have not responded to God, and He is not angry with me, it is no wonder if a man like me does not respond to me and I am longsuffering with him."

12.11.6.en: * One of the brothers complained to an elder, saying: "What shall I do, father, for my brother grieves me because he wanders about?" The elder said: "Bear with him, my beloved, for God will bring him back when He sees your patience and your treatment of him with gentleness and mildness, and put away harshness from you, for a devil does not cast out a devil. And by your gentleness and patience he will return, for God brings a man back only by longsuffering, goodness of heart and forbearance."

12.12.s.en: 9. Evil words and the sweet tongue

12.12.0.en: 13 The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble. 14 A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him.

12.12.1.en: "The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble" [v. 13]

12.12.2.en: Judgment is passed on the wicked on the great day of the Lord through the evil words they uttered. What they carried in their lives of disobedience to the divine commandment, and of lust for evil, condemns them, and they do not escape the nets they set for themselves without knowing it. But the righteous man stands on the great day of the Lord rejoicing; he feels that the troubles, trials and sufferings he endured have become the secret of eternal glory for him.

12.12.3.en: * And do not keep company with the one who has a harsh tongue, nor with the haughty of heart.

12.12.4.en: Anba Paula of Tamouh * An elder said: "If a monk reviles his brother by mentioning some of his sins, such as saying to him: O fornicator, or O thief, or O liar, and the reviled one keeps silent and forgives the reviler, and says in himself: Truly I am a sinner, then the sin for which he was reviled and of which he said that he is a sinner is forgiven him, and it comes upon the reviler, because instead of confessing his own sin he exposed his brother's sin, and because the reviled one bore the exposure of his sin it is counted to him as a confession, and because he forgave his brother he obtained forgiveness."

12.12.5.en: The Paradise of the Fathers * A golden vessel is not used for base things because of its high price, how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so it is not permissible for us to defile it with foul speech, reviling and slander of others.

12.12.6.en: * Silence is a great growth for a man and rest for his soul. Silence gives the heart constant solitude. Silence brings tears to a man, silence drives away anger, silence is the companion of asceticism, silence begets knowledge, silence guards love, silence does not pain any man's heart nor scandalize anyone, silence does its work without murmuring, silence keeps the lips and tongue and leaves nothing of evil in the heart, silence is the perfection of philosophy, and he who holds fast to silence can hold fast to all good things. He who keeps silence with knowledge has been sealed with the seal of Christ, and he who keeps it will without doubt inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.

12.13.0.en: St. John Chrysostom A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him" [14]

12.13.1.en: The wise man often concentrates on the tongue, for the righteous man is filled with good things through his sweet, holy tongue for the account of the Kingdom of God, and what he practices returns to him. So by the tongue as by deed man sows, to reap fruit according to what he sowed. "For whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7).

12.13.2.en: * Silence for God's sake is good, as speaking for God's sake is good.

12.14.s.en: 10. He that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise

12.14.0.en: "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise" [15]

12.14.1.en: The foolish man who lacks divine wisdom is self-reliant; he does not seek God's counsel, nor resort to a father or guide. But the wise man in his humility resorts to God, and consults, not clinging to his opinion without fitting dialogue.

12.14.2.en: * He who relies on his own opinion, even if he is a saint, is deceived, and the danger of his deception is greater than the danger of the beginner who has put his direction in the hands of another.

12.14.3.en: For the first is like a ship's captain who throws himself into a boat without sail or oar in the middle of the sea, relying on his skill and art of management. The second, that is the beginner, is like one who has no experience of sea voyages, and asks a skilled sailor to take him aboard his ship, which is well furnished with all its necessities and needs.

12.14.4.en: Let none of you be deceived and flee from the gentle yoke of obedience, determined to cling to his own opinion in spiritual matters, such as fasting and prayer and other marks of faith and asceticism, supposing that by this he will be saved!

12.14.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * The way of obedience is the shortest of paths, though it is the most difficult. And there is only one way in which, once we walk, we go astray: it is that which we call "reliance on self and on our personal will."

12.14.6.en: * Obedience is a defense before God. If you are asked by Him: Why did you do this? You answer Him: "You, Lord, commanded obedience, and I did what You commanded," and so you answer Him and are justified.

12.14.7.en: Voyaging in this ship carries safety from drowning. Man travels while he sleeps, as a man travels asleep in a ship and is not obliged to steer it, because its steersman is present. Such is the condition of the man walking under obedience: he voyages toward heaven and perfection while he sleeps, without toil and without thinking about what he ought to do. For the superiors are the steersmen of this ship and the ones who watch for him. Truly, it is no small matter but very great. Man crosses the sea of this world upon the forearm and arm of another! This is the great grace which God does to him who walks under obedience.

12.14.8.en: St. John Climacus * Our holy father John began his monastic life with perfect obedience and humility, so that by them he might tear down the roots of sin, and Anba Ammoi disciplined him by the law of the Lord, and all that he taught him he fulfilled and kept the counsel, being very obedient; therefore the grace of God was supporting him.

12.14.9.en: * St. John used to say to the brothers: "Submit in perfect obedience according to the way of life of our fathers. Receive counsel with faith, and especially with humility, purity, the fear of God, steadfastness in God and occupation with Him; these things are higher than all the virtues and make the soul shine with God by its uprightness." The Fathers have related of him that just as the earth cannot fall, so Anba John the Short could not fall because of the greatness of his humility, for he fulfilled great obedience while under submission to his spiritual father, being aflame with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

12.15.s.en: 11. Restraining the spirit of anger and covering others

12.15.0.en: "A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame" [16]

12.15.1.en: * It behooves us to restrain every movement of anger and soften it under the guidance of discernment (wisdom), so that we do not rush into blind rage, of which Solomon said: "The fool shows all his anger, but the wise man quiets it in the end" (Prov 11:29). That is, the foolish man is inflamed with the passion of anger to avenge himself, but the wise man, because of the maturity of his counsel and his gentleness, extinguishes anger little by little and rids himself of it.

12.15.2.en: The Apostle says something similar: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19). That is, do not allow your hearts to be confined in the straits of impatience and cowardice, so that when any violent storm of anger arises you cannot bear it, but let your hearts be wide, receiving the waves of words of anger in the wide currents of love, which "beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 13:7). And so your minds are enlarged with longsuffering and patience, and there are in it the depths of faithful counsel, which receives the smoke of anger and destroys it.

12.15.3.en: The passage can be understood in the following sense: we give place to anger by submitting with a humble and calm mind to the passion of others, and bowing to the impatience of the angry, as though we deserved every kind of wrong (as a discipline for us).

12.15.4.en: As for those who distort the meaning of perfection of which the Apostle speaks, interpreting "give place unto wrath" as withdrawing from a man in the time of his anger, it seems to me that by this they do not cut off the causes of anger, but stir up the motives of strife. For unless we straightway amend the neighbor's anger by an amendment full of humility, withdrawal provokes the neighbor all the more...

12.15.5.en: Solomon speaks of a matter like this, saying: "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). And "Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou do something to the other when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame" (Prov 25:8). In this he does not blame haste in strife in the sense that he praises delayed strife.

12.15.6.en: In the same way we must understand the saying: "A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame" (Prov 12:16), for it does not mean that the wise man stores up the outburst of anger secretly, but blames the outburst of rash anger... He must hide the outburst for this reason, that when he leaves it for a while he calms the spirit of anger forever. For this is the nature of anger, when room is left for it (that is, we are not hasty with it) it weakens and perishes, but if anger is displayed in a state of rage it burns more and more.

12.15.7.en: Hearts must be enlarged and opened so that they are not confined in the straits of cowardice and filled with increasing anger, and become unable to receive the commandments of God, by what the prophet calls "enlargement of the heart or exceeding enlargement." For the prophet says: "I ran in the way of thy commandments when I enlarged my heart" (Ps 119:32).

12.15.8.en: For slowness to anger is wisdom, which we learn from the clear sayings of Holy Scripture, for "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Prov 14:29). Therefore Scripture says of him who asked the Lord for the gift of wisdom: "And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore" (1 Kgs 4:29).

12.15.9.en: Father Joseph The fool in his foolishness exposes others as one better than they, but the wise man covers others.

12.15.10.en: When Noah became drunk and was uncovered, Ham told his two brothers outside (Gen 9:22). But Shem and Japheth took a garment and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father, and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness (Gen 23:9).

12.15.11.en: * Ham the son of Noah brought a curse upon himself, because he laughed when he saw his father's nakedness. But the two who covered their father's nakedness received the blessing.

12.15.12.en: St. Ambrose * Do not say that so-and-so is bad by nature, and so-and-so is good by nature. For if he is good by nature, can he never become bad, and if he is bad by nature, can he never become good? But now we see the change happening quickly from one state to another... This we have seen not only in the Holy Scriptures, I mean that tax collectors became apostles, the disciple became the betrayer of his Master, harlots became chaste, robbers became victors, astrologers became worshippers of God, unbelievers passed over to true worship... This happened in the Old Testament and the New Testament, and every day anyone can see these things happening... So let no one purpose to rebuke another, saying: O wicked one, given over to the passions of sin.

12.15.13.en: * If it is counted evil that a man should not see his own sins, his evil is doubled when he sits on the seat of judgment of others while carrying a beam in his eyes.
